titel: Islamophobia, perception and what we can control

faehigkeiten.grund: Dynamik weder belegt noch ausgeschlossen (Abruf laeuft ueber den Werbedienst podtrac.com) - zu wenig fuer ein Urteil, aber nicht nichts

einzeiler: Haroon Moghul reflects on 25 years of Islamophobia, faith, and spiritual resilience.
kurzfassung: Haroon Moghul looks back on his experience as a student leader at NYU on September 11, 2001, and how it abruptly shaped his life. He discusses the long-term impact of Islamophobia in America, the personal toll of acting as a public spokesperson, and how finding spiritual grounding in Dubai helped him rebuild his life. Ultimately, he argues that focusing on internal responsibility and community-building offers a path forward beyond the politics of grievance.
stichpunkte: Haroon Moghul was heading the Muslim Student Association at NYU when the towers fell on September 11.
Because the student organization was uniquely accessible online, media and outsiders immediately turned to them for answers.
Stepping into a public spokesperson role prevented Moghul from naturally exploring his own relationship with religion in his youth.
Severe burnout and personal hardships in his thirties led him to spend time in Dubai, where anonymity in local mosques brought profound healing.
Experiencing prayer in a Muslim-majority society revealed a deeper, contemplative dimension of faith beyond outward rules.
Moghul compares the cumulative cultural impact of Islamophobia to climate change, noting that moral choices leave lasting damage over time.
He advocates shifting away from defensive political reactions toward constructive actions and focusing on what individuals can control.
beschreibung:
In 2001, just before 9/11, Haroon Moghul was head of the Muslim Student Association at NYU, but he had not yet solidified his own relationship with Islam. Then, everything changed, and he had to navigate his beliefs when islamophobia was suddenly everywhere. He is now a chaplain at Xavier University, and offers his take on shifting the focus away from rampant islamophobia onto what we can control.
